title: Checkpoint, highlight, end stage, end project, lessons and exception reports
blurb: Give the purpose, author, audience and timing of each of the six progress reports, and avoid the classic mix-ups between them.
question: A team manager wants to tell the project manager how a work package is going. Which report should be used, and how often is it produced?

teach.body: The progress practice uses six reports. Two are regular: the checkpoint report (team manager to project manager) and the highlight report (project manager to board). Four are triggered by events: the end stage report, the end project report, the lessons report and the exception report. In plain English: ask who is writing to whom, and whether it is routine or because something has happened.

teach.h: End project report versus lessons report
End stage report: the board's decision pack
teach.body: The end stage report, prepared in managing a stage boundary ('evaluate the stage'), summarizes progress to date and the overall project situation, and gives the board enough information to decide what to do next with the project. When an exception plan is being presented, an end stage report is produced only if the board requires it.

teach.h: Worked scenario: a museum digitization project
teach.body: At Carrow Heritage Trust, imaging team manager Dev Patel sends project manager Lucy Fairweather a checkpoint report every Friday, as the work package requires. Lucy sends the board a highlight report each month. When a scanner failure is forecast to push stage 2 beyond its time tolerance, she sends an exception report. At the end of stage 3 she produces an end stage report, and in closing she writes the end project report and the lessons report.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) Checkpoint reports go to the project manager; highlight reports go to the board. (2) The highlight report is routine; the end stage report supports the end-of-stage decision. (3) The end project report reviews performance against the PID; the lessons report passes lessons on. (4) An issue that stays within tolerance is not a reason for an exception report.

items: Checkpoint: team manager to PM, work package status, frequency in the work package.
Highlight: PM to board, stage status, intervals set by the board.
End stage: PM to board at stage end, to decide what next.
Exception: PM to board when a breach is forecast, with options and a recommendation.
End project: performance against the PID; lessons: passes lessons on.

summary: You can now match each of the six progress reports to its author, audience, timing and purpose, and avoid the classic confusions: checkpoint versus highlight, highlight versus end stage, and end project versus lessons report.

A.q: Which report does a team manager use to report work package status to the project manager?
A.why: The checkpoint report gives the project manager the status of the work package at the frequency defined in the work package.

whyNot.0: The highlight report goes from the project manager to the board.
whyNot.2: The end stage report is the project manager's report at the end of a stage.
whyNot.3: The exception report goes from the project manager to the board when a breach is forecast.

A.q: What is the purpose of a highlight report?
options: To review performance against the PID
To pass on lessons to future projects
To report a forecast tolerance breach
To summarize stage status for the board
A.why: Highlight reports give the project board (and possibly others) a summary of stage status at intervals it defines.

whyNot.0: Reviewing performance against the PID is the end project report.
whyNot.1: Passing on lessons is the lessons report.
whyNot.2: Reporting a forecast tolerance breach is the exception report.

A.q: Which report reviews how the project performed against the version of the PID used to authorize it?
A.why: The end project report reviews performance against the PID version used to authorize the project.

whyNot.1: The end stage report covers progress to date and supports the next-stage decision.
whyNot.2: The lessons report passes on lessons rather than reviewing performance against the PID.
whyNot.3: The highlight report summarizes current stage status.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. The [?] report gives a summary of progress to date and enough information for the board to decide what to do next with the project.
B.why: The end stage report summarizes progress and the overall situation so the board can decide what to do next.

whyNot.0: The highlight report is a routine status summary, not the end-of-stage decision pack.
whyNot.1: The checkpoint report covers a work package and goes to the project manager.
whyNot.3: The exception report addresses a forecast breach with options and a recommendation.

B.q:
Which two statements about the exception report are correct?
1. It is produced by the project manager for the project board.
2. It is produced at intervals defined by the board.
3. It offers options and a recommendation.
4. It is produced by the team manager when a work package is late.
B.why: The project manager sends the exception report to the board (1), and it offers options and a recommendation (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: exception reports are event-driven, not periodic.
whyNot.2: Both are false: it is not periodic, and team managers escalate to the PM as an issue.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: the exception report is the project manager's product.

B.q: A project manager needs to tell the board that a stage is forecast to exceed its cost tolerance. Which report should be used?
B.why: The exception report informs the board when a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance.

whyNot.0: A highlight report is routine; a forecast breach needs its own exception report.
whyNot.1: An issue report records a formal issue; it does not escalate a stage breach to the board.
whyNot.2: The end stage report is produced at the end of a stage, not when a breach is forecast.

C.q: Which report is produced in controlling a stage at intervals defined by the board, and who writes it?
options: End stage report; the project manager
C.why: The project manager produces highlight reports in controlling a stage ('report highlights') at the board's intervals.

whyNot.0: Checkpoint reports come from managing product delivery at the frequency in the work package.
whyNot.2: The end stage report is produced in managing a stage boundary.
whyNot.3: Exception reports are produced by the project manager, and only when a breach is forecast.

C.q: In which process are the end project report and the lessons report prepared, and by whom?
options: Closing a project; the project manager
Managing a stage boundary; the project board
Controlling a stage; the project support
C.why: In closing a project ('evaluate the project') the project manager prepares the end project report and the lessons report.

whyNot.1: In directing a project the board uses the end project report to authorize closure; it does not write it.
whyNot.2: Managing a stage boundary produces the end stage report; the board does not write reports.
whyNot.3: Controlling a stage produces highlight and exception reports, and the PM writes them.

C.q: A project manager uses the highlight report to ask the board to authorize the next stage. Why is this a confusion?
options: Highlight reports go to the team managers
Stage authorization needs a checkpoint report
The end stage report supports that decision
The exception report supports that decision
C.why: The end stage report, produced at the end of the stage, gives the board the information to decide what to do next.

whyNot.0: Highlight reports go to the project board, not to team managers.
whyNot.1: Checkpoint reports go from team managers to the PM and play no part in stage authorization.
whyNot.3: The exception report deals with a forecast breach, not routine stage authorization.

reteach.title: Reports in a restaurant
reteach.question: How would the six reports look in a busy restaurant kitchen?

blocks.body: Section chefs tell the head chef how their station is doing every hour (checkpoint). The head chef sends the owner a weekly summary (highlight). If food costs will blow the budget, the head chef tells the owner at once with options (exception). At the end of the season, the head chef reviews the season and asks what next (end stage). When the restaurant closes for good, there is a final review (end project) and notes for future openings (lessons).

blocks.text: The section chef never writes to the owner directly: checkpoint reports go to the project manager, not to the board.

explain.body: Team manager to project manager: work package status, including its issues and risks, at the frequency in the work package.

test.q: How often are checkpoint reports produced?
options: At intervals set by the project board
At the end of every stage of the project
At the frequency in the work package
When a breach of tolerance is forecast
test.why: Checkpoint reports are produced at the frequency defined in the work package.

whyNot.0: Intervals set by the board apply to highlight reports.
whyNot.1: Stage end reporting is the end stage report.
whyNot.3: A forecast breach triggers an exception report or an issue, not a checkpoint report.

explain.body: Project manager to board (and possibly other stakeholders): a summary of stage status at intervals the board defines.

test.why: Highlight reports go from the project manager to the project board, and possibly other stakeholders.

whyNot.1: Team managers write checkpoint reports; they are not the audience for highlight reports.
whyNot.2: Project support may help compile reports but is not their audience.
whyNot.3: Quality assurance is independent of the project and is not the report's audience.

explain.body: Project manager to board when a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance, with consequences, options and a recommendation.

test.q: When is an exception report produced?
options: At the end of each stage of the project
When a work package has been completed
At intervals defined by the project board
When tolerance is forecast to be exceeded
test.why: An exception report informs the board when a stage or project plan is forecast to exceed tolerance.

whyNot.0: Stage ends call for an end stage report.
whyNot.1: Completed work packages are notified to the PM; no exception report is needed.
whyNot.2: Regular intervals apply to highlight reports.

explain.body: The end project report reviews performance against the PID used to authorize the project. The lessons report passes on lessons for other projects.

test.q: What is the purpose of the lessons report?
options: To summarize stage status for the board
To pass on lessons that other projects can use
To review performance against the PID
To record informal issues and observations
test.why: The lessons report passes on lessons from the project so that they can be applied on other or future projects.

whyNot.0: A summary of stage status for the board is a highlight report.
whyNot.2: Reviewing performance against the PID is the end project report.
whyNot.3: Informal issues and observations are recorded in the daily log.
